title: How block ciphers think
syllabusUnit: Unit II: Block Cipher Principles & Feistel Structure
covers: Block vs stream, confusion & diffusion, Feistel, S-DES, design principles
learningGoals: You will be able to distinguish block ciphers from stream ciphers.
You will be able to define Shannon's concepts of Confusion and Diffusion.
You will be able to trace a round through a Feistel network.

lessonCards.title: Block vs Stream Ciphers
lessonCards.analogy: A shipping container loaded in 64-bit crates vs a garden hose spraying bits continuously.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Block ciphers process fixed-size chunks of data (e.g. 128 bits) at a time. Stream ciphers encrypt one bit or byte at a time on the fly.
lessonCards.example: AES processes 128-bit blocks; ChaCha20 generates a continuous keystream.

lessonCards.title: Confusion and Diffusion
lessonCards.analogy: Confusion is turning letters into a foggy puzzle; Diffusion is dropping food dye that spreads across the entire pool.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Confusion obscures the relationship between the key and the ciphertext (via S-boxes). Diffusion spreads single plaintext bit changes across all ciphertext bits (via P-boxes).
lessonCards.example: Changing 1 bit in the input scrambles ~64 bits in the output.

lessonCards.title: The Feistel Network
lessonCards.analogy: Splitting a deck into left and right halves, transforming one half, and swapping them round by round.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Horst Feistel's brilliant design: splits data into L and R. R_new = L XOR F(R, RoundKey); L_new = R. Decryption runs the exact same code with keys reversed!
lessonCards.example: DES, Blowfish, and Twofish all use Feistel networks.

questions.prompt: What makes a Feistel cipher network uniquely practical for hardware implementation?
options: Decryption uses the identical circuit architecture as encryption, just reversing subkeys
questions.explanation: Because L and R swap each round with XOR, the round function F does NOT need to be invertible; running keys in reverse order decrypts automatically.
wrongExplanations: Correct! The exact same hardware handles encryption and decryption.
All silicon circuits require electric power.
Feistel rounds apply XOR, substitution, and permutation.
Feistel structures scale to 64, 128, and 256 bits.
questions.realWorldExample: DES and Triple-DES use 16-round Feistel structures.

questions.prompt: In cryptographic design, what component is primarily responsible for introducing CONFUSION?
questions.explanation: S-boxes provide non-linear substitution, making the mathematical relationship between key and ciphertext complicated and non-linear.
wrongExplanations: Correct! S-boxes provide confusion.
Permutation P-boxes provide diffusion.
XOR with 0 leaves bits unchanged.
Counters are used in CTR mode.
questions.realWorldExample: S-box design determines a block cipher's resistance to differential cryptanalysis.

questions.prompt: What component is primarily responsible for introducing DIFFUSION in a block cipher?
questions.explanation: Permutations and linear transformations spread the influence of single input bits across multiple output bits.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Permutations distribute influence across the entire block.
S-boxes specialize in local non-linear confusion.
Clock oscillators control CPU timing.
Random seeds initialize PRNGs.
questions.realWorldExample: AES uses ShiftRows and MixColumns to achieve complete block diffusion in two rounds.

questions.prompt: In a standard Feistel round with input halves (L0, R0), what is the formula for the right output half R1?
questions.explanation: R1 = L0 XOR F(R0, K1), while L1 = R0.
wrongExplanations: Correct! The round function output is XORed with the left half.
Simple addition overflows without Feistel properties.
Multiplication is not standard Feistel logic.
L0 must be combined with the function output.
questions.realWorldExample: This exact formula was designed by Horst Feistel at IBM in the 1970s.

questions.prompt: How many bits are in a single standard block processed by DES and Simplified DES (S-DES)?
options: DES is 64 bits; S-DES is 8 bits
DES is 1024 bits; S-DES is 512 bits
DES is 1 bit; S-DES is 2 bits
questions.explanation: Standard DES processes 64-bit blocks. Educational S-DES processes 8-bit blocks with 10-bit keys.
wrongExplanations: Correct! DES = 64-bit block; S-DES = 8-bit block.
1024 bits is common for RSA keys, not DES blocks.
1 bit is a stream cipher unit.
256 bits is common for AES-256.
questions.realWorldExample: S-DES was created by Edward Schaefer to teach students Feistel rounds without massive 64-bit tables.

questions.prompt: Why does a pure stream cipher require that a keystream NEVER repeat?
options: Reusing keystream allows attackers to XOR ciphertexts and recover plaintexts
A repeating keystream deletes hard drives
Stream ciphers only run on Saturdays
questions.explanation: Like the One-Time Pad, reusing keystream K on messages A and B allows calculating (A XOR K) XOR (B XOR K) = A XOR B.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Keystream reuse destroys confidentiality.
Software does not erase hardware.
Days of the week are irrelevant.
Keystreams can generate millions of bytes.
questions.realWorldExample: The WEP Wi-Fi protocol was broken because IVs were too short, causing keystream reuse.

ashRecap: Block ciphers mix Confusion (S-boxes) and Diffusion (P-boxes). Feistel networks make decrypting as easy as running the round keys backward!
